rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.4 and 3 - the authors inoculated 60 potted cucumber seedlings in a Beijing greenhouse, imaged them daily with a FluorCam chlorophyll fluorescence system for 10 days, and trained an improved ResNet50 classifier on 557 original (7798 augmented) images; Table 3 and Fig. 17 report their own classification accuracies (94.76% overall; 84.59% at 4 DPI).
rows.notes: The study only shows that chlorophyll fluorescence imaging plus a CNN can distinguish inoculated-but-asymptomatic cucumber seedlings from healthy ones about 3-4 days before visible symptoms, and that Ft_D3 and Fv/Fm images show lesion-corresponding spots (Fig. 10, Fig. 18). It reports no result on using such maps to target pesticide application to afflicted areas, nor any measurement of reduced chemical consumption or environmental effect; the Discussion only asserts the approach 'may be more effective and cost-efficient' than removing infected parts. Detection is a precondition of the claimed site-specific pesticide use, so upstream. Note also the sensing is proximal (camera 40 cm above potted seedlings in a greenhouse), not field-scale remote sensing producing spatial distribution maps; Discussion states constraints for field settings and large greenhouses (parameter count, slow inference).

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a greenhouse seedling-stage detection experiment with a single cultivar, single site and single pathogen; it provides no evidence on pesticide targeting or chemical-use reduction.
